prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Because there are avenues Of traffic lights, a phone book Of brothers and lawyers, Why should you think your purse Will not be tugged from your arm Or the screen door Will remain latched Against the man Who hugs and kisses His pillow In the corridor of loneliness? There is a window of light A sprinkler turning As the earth turns, And you do not think of the hills And of the splintered wrists it takes To give you The heat rising toward the ceiling. You expect your daughter To be at the door any moment And your husband to arrive With the night That is suddenly all around. You expect the stove to burst A collar of fire When you want it, The siamese cats To move against your legs, purring. But remember this: Because blood revolves from one lung to the next, Why think it will After tonight?

prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The poem examines the fragility of ordinary safety and domestic expectation by contrasting everyday comforts with images of violence, loneliness, labor, and bodily vulnerability. It reveals that what seems reliable—home, family, warmth, even breath and circulation—can vanish at any moment, underscoring the uncertainty beneath daily life.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Because, Why, Will

outputs.L1:
Because there are avenues  
of traffic lights, a phone book  
of brothers and lawyers,  
why should you think your purse  
will not be tugged from your arm,  
or that the screen door  
will remain latched  
against the man  
who hugs and kisses  
his pillow  
in the corridor of loneliness?

There is a window of light,  
a sprinkler turning  
as the earth turns,  
and you do not think of the hills,  
or of the splintered wrists it takes  
to give you  
the heat rising toward the ceiling.

You expect your daughter  
to be at the door any moment,  
and your husband to arrive  
with the night  
that is suddenly all around.

You expect the stove to burst  
into a collar of fire  
when you want it,  
the Siamese cats  
to move against your legs, purring.

But remember this:  
because blood revolves  
from one lung to the next,  
why think it will  
after tonight?
outputs.L2:
Since streets are lined with stoplights,  
and directories are filled with the names  
of siblings and attorneys,  
what makes you believe your handbag  
will not be yanked away,  
or that the screen door  
will stay fastened  
against the stranger  
who embraces and kisses  
his pillow  
in the hallway of isolation?

Somewhere a lit window shines.  
A sprinkler rotates  
while the planet itself keeps turning,  
and you give no thought to the hills,  
or to the broken wrists required  
to bring you  
the warmth gathering near the ceiling.

You assume your daughter  
will appear at the door soon.  
You assume your husband  
will come home  
with the darkness  
that has abruptly settled everywhere.  
You count on the stove  
to flare up  
with a ring of flame  
whenever you ask it to,  
and on the Siamese cats  
to brush against your ankles,  
softly purring.

But keep this in mind:  
just because blood moves  
from one lung to the other,  
why should you believe  
it will continue  
after this night?
outputs.L3:
The poem questions the comforting assumption that ordinary routines and protections can keep danger at a distance. It suggests that the familiar structures people rely on—home, family, daily habits, and a sense of safety—are not as secure as they may seem. Rather than presenting domestic life as a place of simple peace, the poem exposes how fragile that peace can be.

A central contrast in the poem is between everyday domestic comfort and the hidden suffering or violence that may exist beneath it. Images of warmth, shelter, and routine are set against an awareness of pain, fear, or harm that is often unseen. In this way, the poem challenges the idea that comfort is natural or guaranteed. What appears safe on the surface may depend on struggles that remain invisible.

The speaker emphasizes that much of what people take for granted is supported by unseen labor and suffering. The warmth of a home, the security of family life, and the ordinary continuation of daily existence may all rely on effort, endurance, and sacrifice that are not always acknowledged. The poem therefore asks readers to look more closely at the conditions beneath comfort and to recognize the vulnerability that lies behind familiar forms of safety.

Expectations surrounding family, home, and protection are also portrayed as uncertain. The poem does not present these things as permanent or dependable. Instead, it shows how easily they can be disturbed by violence, loss, or fear. What people imagine as stable—the household, the body, the future—can quickly become unstable.

The final lines deepen this warning by suggesting that even life’s most basic continuities cannot be assumed to last. Breathing, blood flow, and the simple fact of being alive are presented as fragile processes rather than certainties. By ending on this note, the poem reminds readers that security is never absolute. The ordinary world may feel protected, but beneath that feeling is a constant awareness of danger, mortality, and the precariousness of life itself.
outputs.L4:
The poem explores the fragility of ordinary safety by placing familiar comforts beside images of danger, exhaustion, and bodily vulnerability. It begins from the world of daily life: the home, the family, warmth, work, and the routines that often make existence feel stable. These details suggest a domestic order in which people expect shelter, connection, and continuity. Yet the poem steadily unsettles that expectation. Against the comfort of the household, it introduces reminders of violence, loneliness, physical labor, and the human body’s dependence on breath and circulation. In doing so, the poem shows that safety is not as permanent or secure as it appears.

This contrast gives the poem much of its emotional force. Ordinary life is presented not as something separate from suffering, but as something constantly shadowed by it. The home may seem protective, but it cannot fully defend against loss. Family may suggest belonging, but it does not erase isolation. Warmth may promise comfort, but it can disappear. Even the body itself, which people often take for granted, is shown to be delicate and uncertain. Breath, blood, and physical strength become reminders that life depends on processes that can fail at any moment.

Through these tensions, the poem challenges the reader’s trust in everyday stability. It suggests that what appears reliable—domestic routine, human closeness, physical health, and the simple continuation of life—is always vulnerable to interruption. The poem does not merely describe fear or suffering; it reveals how closely such possibilities exist beneath ordinary experience. By bringing together comfort and threat, it exposes the hidden uncertainty within daily life and asks the reader to recognize how fragile even the most familiar forms of security can be.
outputs.L5: Why will tomorrow be better than today? Because every new day gives us a chance to learn, grow, and make different choices. We will face challenges, but we will also discover new opportunities. Because we keep trying, we become stronger. Why should we believe in the future? Because hope helps us move forward, and our actions today will shape what comes next.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in a dark, surreal, mid-century American style about domestic safety, urban danger, loneliness, and the fragility of ordinary expectations.
counterfactuals.output:
The latch believes in morning.  
It clicks with the small authority  
of a man in a hat  
who has never missed a train.

Inside, the kitchen glows  
like a safe deposit box.  
Cups hang by their handles,  
white and obedient.  
The toaster crouches chrome and patient,  
a little animal trained not to bite.  
On the table, the bread waits  
for its transformation  
into something warm enough  
to trust.

But the city is breathing under the door.

It comes up through the floorboards,  
through the telephone’s black mouth,  
through the radio where men  
with polished voices  
announce calamity  
between advertisements for soap.  
A siren combs the avenues.  
A woman laughs in an alley  
and the laugh breaks in half.  
Somewhere a shoe lies on its side  
beside a puddle bright as an eye.

We have been told what walls are for.  
We have believed in curtains,  
in milk bottles,  
in the square assurance of windows.  
We have believed the lamp  
could make a circle  
and call it home.

Yet every evening  
the room tilts slightly  
toward the street.  
The coat on the chair becomes a stranger.  
The clock practices its tiny murder.  
The mirror holds still  
as if waiting to identify us.

At supper, the knife shines  
with civic discipline.  
The salt stands in its glass tower.  
The plates are moons  
with nothing on them  
but the old hunger  
orbiting quietly.

No one knocks.

That is the worst of it.

No fist at the door,  
no telegram,  
no face pressed flat  
against the pane—  
only the refrigerator humming  
like a distant factory,  
only the bed prepared  
with its cold white flag,  
only the knowledge  
that danger does not always enter.

Sometimes it is already seated  
in the parlor,  
crossing its legs,  
wearing your slippers,  
turning the pages of yesterday’s paper  
with careful, domestic hands.

And outside,  
the city lifts its iron shoulders.  
Neon bleeds in the rain.  
Taxis pass like yellow warnings.  
Each window floats alone  
in its black aquarium,  
each life arranged behind glass  
around a table, a lamp,  
a silence.

We expect the kettle to boil.  
We expect the key to fit.  
We expect the heart  
to continue its anonymous labor  
in the chest.

How delicate these arrangements are—  
a child’s tower of blocks  
on the edge of the elevated tracks.

One tremor,  
one missed step,  
one shadow separating itself  
from the shadow it belonged to,

and the evening opens,  
not like a door,  
but like a wound  
that had been painted  
the color of a door.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a literary poem that begins with “Because there are avenues” and uses images like traffic lights, a phone book, a purse being tugged, a screen door, a sprinkler, a daughter, a husband, a stove, Siamese cats, and blood circulating.
counterfactuals.output:
Because there are avenues where traffic lights  
hang like small, stern moons above our waiting,  
I learned to love the pause before arrival,  
the red command, the green forgiveness.

In the phone book of the city, names sleep  
pressed thin as leaves—  
every lost husband, every daughter  
married into another weather,  
every voice that might answer  
if the past still had a number.

Once, in a market bright with oranges,  
I felt my purse being tugged  
and turned to find only a child’s hand,  
or my own fear, or the century  
wanting what little I carried.

At home the screen door slapped shut  
with its summer reprimand.  
A sprinkler worried the lawn  
in silver parentheses,  
and the stove breathed blue flowers  
under the blackened pot.

Our Siamese cats moved through the rooms  
like questions with tails,  
their eyes two drops of old varnish,  
their silence inherited from temples  
no one in our family had seen.

My daughter stood barefoot in the kitchen,  
holding a spoon as if it were a wand,  
and my husband, reading the news,  
lifted his face into the ordinary light—  
that fragile kingdom we mistook  
for furniture, for duty, for evening.

All the while, beneath our speech,  
blood was circulating,  
dark river, loyal engine,  
carrying salt and heat  
from one locked chamber to another,  
as if the body believed  
every departure  
was only another way home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a tense, ominous poem addressed to “you,” where everyday household comforts gradually become uncertain and the final lines question whether life will continue after tonight.
counterfactuals.output:
You lock the door the way you always do,  
a small bright click against the dark.  
The kettle settles on the stove,  
the lamp pours honey over the room,  
your slippers wait with their soft mouths open.

For a while, everything remembers its name.  
The table is only a table.  
The chair keeps still beneath your coat.  
The clock lifts its careful hand  
and sets it down again.

But the house has begun to listen.

The radiator knocks once, then pauses,  
as if deciding whether to answer.  
The curtains breathe against the glass  
though no wind moves outside.  
In the cupboard, plates lean closer together,  
whispering their white, ceramic prayers.

You tell yourself the shadows always gather  
in the corners first.  
You tell yourself the floorboards always sigh  
when the night grows heavy.  
You tell yourself the mirror in the hall  
has always held your face  
a second too long.

The bed is turned down, waiting.  
The sheets are clean and cold.  
Your pillow keeps the shape  
of someone you have not been  
for years.

Downstairs, the refrigerator hums  
like a throat trying not to speak.  
A spoon ticks in the sink.  
The walls press inward by degrees,  
so gently you could call it weather,  
so slowly you could call it home.

And now the light above you flickers.  
And now the lock clicks softly back.  
And now the room grows still enough  
to hear the dark come through the cracks.

Tell me—  
when the last lamp empties itself,  
when the house forgets your name,  
will morning find you breathing?

Will anything continue  
after tonight?
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an imitation of a confessional/free verse poem with long enjambed lines, unsettling domestic imagery, and a refrain-like logic built around “Because…” and “Why think…?”
counterfactuals.output:
Because the sink is full of little moons, each spoon turning its back  
on the overhead light, because the dish towel has stiffened  
into the shape of a hand that would not let go,

because the house at night keeps making its soft corrections—  
the refrigerator clearing its throat, the pipes confessing  
to water they have already lost, the floorboards saying  
not here, not here, though I am standing on them—

why think the body is any different from a cupboard  
with one bad hinge, opening a little in the dark  
to show the stacked white plates of its intentions?

Because I have stood in the kitchen eating cold beans from the can  
with the can opener still attached like a small metal animal  
biting the rim, because I have listened to the clock  
divide the room into before and after and after and after,

why think forgiveness comes in a clean shirt, folded  
at the foot of the bed, smelling of soap and weather?

Because the laundry basket is full of everyone I have been  
and none of them are dry, because the bathmat remembers  
each wet footprint more tenderly than I do,

because the mirror above the sink keeps returning my face  
as if it were a borrowed object I have failed to polish,  
why think I was ever alone in that room?

The cabinets swell in August. The bread goes blue in its bag.  
A fly beats itself against the window with the patience of a saint  
or a prisoner, and the child in the photograph on the fridge  
holds up a paper sun with all its yellow fingers spread.

Because the oven light is on though nothing is baking,  
because inside it the racks gleam like ribs,  
because I have opened the door just to feel the heat  
of something waiting to be useful,

why think hunger is only the wish to be filled?

Because my mother’s voice lives in the broom closet  
among the light bulbs and old batteries, because sometimes  
when I reach for the dustpan she says my name  
with the tired mercy of a match struck in a storm,

because my father’s silence sits in the armchair  
wearing the dent of his body better than he ever did,

why think the dead are finished with furniture?

I have made a bed so carefully it looked accused.  
I have tucked the corners under until the sheet was smooth  
as a frozen pond, and still, by morning,  
there was the old evidence: the twisted blanket, the pillow  
creased by the weight of my unreliable head.

Because the knife block keeps its dark mouths open,  
because the lemons harden in the bowl like small, sour hearts,  
because the dog dreams under the table and whimpers  
at whatever door will not open,

why think love should be kind to be real?

There is a stain on the ceiling shaped like a country  
no one admits leaving. There is a crack in the teacup  
that sings when the water is boiling. There is dust  
on the wedding album, dust in the piano, dust  
making a soft republic under the bed.

Because I have swept the same corner for years  
and still something gathers there, gray and intimate,  
because the window shows me the neighbor’s window  
and in it a woman rinsing a red cup again and again,

why think repetition is not a form of prayer?

Because I was taught to smile while carrying the trash out,  
to thank the door for closing, to call the bruise  
a shadow, the shouting weather, the locked room privacy,

because I learned to set the table for absence—  
fork, knife, glass, napkin, the chair pulled back  
as if anyone might arrive hungry enough to change me—

why think survival is not also a ceremony  
with no guests and no music, only the fluorescent hum  
and the kettle beginning, despite everything, to cry?
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal narrative poem about a woman at home at night expecting her family to return, while the poem meditates on crime, heat, loneliness, and mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
At midnight the house began to sweat.

Not the walls only,  
not the blue throat of the refrigerator  
humming its one cold hymn,  
but the framed faces in the hallway,  
the locked glass of the windows,  
the floorboards remembering forests  
and sighing sap.

She had left the porch light on  
for her husband and the children,  
who were late from wherever roads go  
when they go dark.

On the stove, the soup had formed a skin.  
It trembled when trucks passed  
like an old witness trying not to speak.

Outside, the heat lay over the neighborhood  
with its full weight—  
a criminal with one hand over every mouth.  
The air smelled of tar, cut grass,  
and something metallic she could not name.  
A siren rose three streets away  
then folded itself back into the city,  
as if even danger had grown tired.

She moved from room to room  
touching ordinary things:

the chair with her son’s jacket  
slumped across it,  
the plastic horse with one leg missing,  
the book her daughter had left open  
to a page where a princess slept  
inside a tower of thorns.

In the bedroom mirror,  
her own face floated toward her  
from a country of silver weather.  
Behind it, the bed waited,  
white and wide,  
an ambulance with no driver.

She thought of crime.

Not only the knife, the gun,  
the sudden hand in an alley,  
the stranger stepping out of shadow  
as if born there—

but the smaller thefts:  
time taking the milk teeth,  
summer stealing the cool from the sheets,  
marriage lifting one’s young body  
and replacing it, gently,  
with another.

The clock clicked its tongue.  
Each second entered the room  
wearing black shoes.

She opened the back door  
and the yard stared in:  
the grass flattened by heat,  
the moon caught in the birdbath,  
pale as a drowned coin.  
Moths beat themselves  
against the porch lamp’s fevered glass,  
soft little catastrophes  
in wedding clothes.

“Come home,” she said,  
but softly,  
because the night was listening  
with a burglar’s ear.

Then the house changed.

The hallway lengthened  
until it became a road.  
The family photographs unhooked themselves  
and walked away carrying their frames  
like suitcases.  
In the kitchen, the knives  
stood upright in the drawer,  
a jury of small bright men.  
The soup whispered her name  
in the voice of her mother,  
dead seven summers and always cold.

She sat at the table.

The table was a boat.  
The house was a sea.  
The ceiling fan turned above her  
like a slow black flower,  
stirring no relief, only the idea  
of relief.

She imagined her family driving home  
through the hot dark,  
their faces lit green by the dashboard,  
the children asleep with open mouths,  
her husband’s hands on the wheel  
as if holding the future in place.

But she also imagined  
the ditch.

The deer.

The red light not obeyed.

The stranger at the gas station  
with his eyes like locked rooms.

Every mother is partly a coroner,  
she thought,  
counting the living again and again,  
making sure no one has vanished  
into the official silence.

A police helicopter  
dragged its white eye over the roofs.  
For one moment the yard flashed open:  
garden hose coiled like a sleeping snake,  
trash cans sweating,  
her shadow nailed to the grass.

Then darkness returned,  
having found nothing  
or having chosen not to say.

She pressed her palm  
to the window.

The glass was warm.  
It felt almost human,  
almost feverish,  
as if the night itself were ill  
and she had been asked to keep vigil.

Loneliness sat across from her  
wearing her husband’s shirt.  
It poured a glass of water.  
It did not drink.

Mortality stood in the doorway  
with the patient manners  
of someone expected eventually.  
It removed its hat.  
It smiled without cruelty.

Still, she waited.

Because waiting was the work  
given to the living:  
to keep the soup from burning,  
to leave a light burning,  
to believe tires will turn  
out of the dark like moons,  
to believe keys will worry the lock,  
to believe the dead are delayed  
but the beloved are merely late.

At last—  
or almost at last—  
headlights spilled across the ceiling.

The house inhaled.

The knives lay down.  
The photographs slipped back  
into their nailed positions.  
The moon climbed out of the birdbath  
and returned, dripping, to the sky.

She rose so quickly  
her chair fell backward  
with the sound of a verdict.

But when she opened the door,  
there was only the empty street  
shining in the heat,  
and a stray dog at the curb  
looking past her into the house  
as though someone inside  
had called its name.

Behind her, the telephone rang.

Once.

Then again.

Each ring a black seed  
dropped into the room.

She stood between the door  
and the ringing,  
between the road and the voice,  
between all that might still arrive  
and all that had already happened.

And the night leaned close,  
hot, criminal, endless,  
breathing against her ear  
like a family  
trying to find its way home.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
